claim: Flagellated bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, sense chemicals in their environment by a chemoreceptor and relay the signals via a well-characterized signaling pathway to the flagellar motor.
source: It is well known that flagellated bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, sense chemicals in their environment by a chemoreceptor and relay the signals via a well-characterized signaling pathway to the flagellar motor.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and is presented as well-known information in the field.

claim: Signals from chemoreceptors change the rotation bias of the motor without influencing the motor speed.
source: It is widely accepted that the signals change the rotation bias of the motor without influencing the motor speed.
evidence: This claim represents the established view in the field that the authors are challenging.

claim: Bacteria are capable of modulating motor speed on merely sensing a ligand.
source: Here, we present results to the contrary and show that the bacteria is also capable of modulating motor speed on merely sensing a ligand.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Step changes in concentration of non-metabolizable ligand cause temporary recruitment of stator units leading to a momentary increase in motor speeds.
source: Step changes in concentration of non-metabolizable ligand cause temporary recruitment of stator units leading to a momentary increase in motor speeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tethered cell experiments and fluorescence measurements shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: For metabolizable ligand, the combined effect of sensing and metabolism leads to higher motor speeds for longer durations.
source: For metabolizable ligand, the combined effect of sensing and metabolism leads to higher motor speeds for longer durations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing glucose (metabolizable) and 2Dg (non-metabolizable) responses.

claim: Bacteria can execute a net directed migration in response to external chemical cues, a phenomenon termed chemotaxis.
source: It is well known that bacteria can execute a net directed migration in response to external chemical cues, a phenomenon termed chemotaxis (Adler, 1966; Berg, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: Escherichia coli is one of the most commonly studied bacteria for understanding chemotaxis.
source: One of the most commonly studied bacteria for understanding chemotaxis is Escherichia coli (Wadhams and Armitage, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: E. coli transmit signals from the environment via a well-characterized signaling pathway to reversible flagellar motors that drive extended helical appendages called flagella thereby achieving locomotion.
source: On sensing a ligand, these bacteria transmit the signal from the environment via a well-characterized signaling pathway to reversible flagellar motors that drive extended helical appendages called flagella thereby achieving locomotion (Adler, 1969; Berg, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: The motor is powered by a proton flux, termed proton motive force (PMF), through an electrochemical gradient of protons across the inner cytoplasmic membrane.
source: The motor is powered by a proton flux, termed proton motive force (PMF), through an electrochemical gradient of protons across the inner cytoplasmic membrane (Fung and Berg, 1995; Gabel and Berg, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When all flagella rotate in the counterclockwise (CCW) direction, the flagella collect into a single bundle leading to a forward motion called a run.
source: When all flagella rotate in the counterclockwise (CCW) direction (as seen from the flagellar end), the flagella collect into a single bundle leading to a forward motion called a run, whereas when one or more of the flagella rotate in the clockwise (CW) direction, they separate from the bundle leading to an abrupt change in direction, also known as a tumble (Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to foundational work.

claim: When one or more of the flagella rotate in the clockwise (CW) direction, they separate from the bundle leading to an abrupt change in direction, also known as a tumble.
source: When all flagella rotate in the counterclockwise (CCW) direction (as seen from the flagellar end), the flagella collect into a single bundle leading to a forward motion called a run, whereas when one or more of the flagella rotate in the clockwise (CW) direction, they separate from the bundle leading to an abrupt change in direction, also known as a tumble (Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to foundational work.

claim: By modulating the duration of runs and tumbles, bacteria achieve a net motion toward chemoattractants or away from chemorepellents.
source: By modulating the duration of runs and tumbles, the bacteria achieve a net motion toward chemoattractants or away from chemorepellents (Brown and Berg, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to foundational work.

claim: The direction of rotation of the flagellar motor is controlled by the switch complex comprising of proteins FliG, FliM, and FliN, which are present at the cytoplasmic end of the motor.
source: The direction of rotation of the flagellar motor is controlled by the switch complex comprising of proteins FliG, FliM, and FliN, which are present at the cytoplasmic end of the motor (Figure 1; Yamaguchi et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: When CheY-P binds to the motor protein FliM, the motor is biased in the CW direction.
source: When CheY-P, the phosphorylated state of the chemotaxis protein CheY, binds to the motor protein FliM, the motor is biased in the CW direction (Welch et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The null state of the motor is the CCW direction.
source: The null state of the motor, however, is the CCW direction.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: When a ligand binds to a chemoreceptor protein, the activity of the chemotaxis pathway protein CheA is reduced, which in turn reduces the production of phosphorylated CheY-P.
source: When a ligand binds to a chemoreceptor protein present in the periplasm, the activity of the chemotaxis pathway protein CheA is reduced, which in turn reduces the production of phosphorylated CheY-P.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the chemotaxis pathway.

claim: A feedback control mechanism intrinsic to the signaling network brings back the phosphorylation state of CheA and CheY to the pre-stimulus levels and resets the duration of CW and CCW rotations to the initial state, a characteristic feature termed perfect adaptation.
source: For ligand concentrations in the nanomolar to the micromolar range, a feedback control mechanism intrinsic to the signaling network brings back the phosphorylation state of CheA and CheY to the pre-stimulus levels and resets the duration of CW and CCW rotations to the initial state, a characteristic feature of the network termed perfect adaptation (Masson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The torque of the flagellar motor is generated via ion flow through at least 11 membrane-bound stator units comprising of proteins, MotA and MotB.
source: The torque of the flagellar motor is generated via ion flow through at least 11 membrane-bound stator units comprising of proteins, MotA and MotB (Yuan and Berg, 2008; Reid et al., 2006; Khan et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated the discrete nature of torque generation by restoring the motility of paralyzed cells by induced expression of wild-type genes from plasmids, causing a step-wise increase in motor speed, a process termed 'resurrection'.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated the discrete nature of torque generation by restoring the motility of paralyzed cells (mot mutants) by induced expression of wild-type (WT) genes from plasmids. The latter caused a step-wise increase in motor speed, a process termed 'resurrection' (Block and Berg, 1984; Blair and Berg, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The number of bound stator units vary with PMF with almost all stator units leaving the motor following removal of PMF.
source: Recent experiments have shown that the number of bound stator units vary with PMF with almost all stator units leaving the motor following removal of PMF (Tipping et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Bacteria are able to vary the number of motor-bound stator units depending on the external mechanical load.
source: Consequently, the bacteria is able to vary the number of motor-bound stator units depending on the external mechanical load (Tipping et al., 2013a; Lele et al., 2013; Nord et al., 2017; Wadhwa et al., 2019) although not all binding sites are necessarily occupied even at high load conditions due to the transient nature of stator unit binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The speed of the motor is controlled via the intracellular concentration of the second messenger cyclic diguanosine monophosphate (c-di-GMP), whose concentration increases during nutrient depletion conditions.
source: In addition to the torque variation with load, the speed of the motor is also controlled via the intracellular concentration of the second messenger cyclic diguanosine monophosphate (c-di-GMP), whose concentration increases during nutrient depletion conditions (Boehm et al., 2010; Paul et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: c-di-GMP binds to the YcgR protein, which in turn interacts with the MotA to reduce the rotation speed of the motor.
source: The c-di-GMP binds to the YcgR protein, a PilZ domain protein, which in turn interacts with the MotA to reduce the rotation speed of the motor.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: There is no clear evidence of the chemosensory transduction system influencing the motor speed in E. coli.
source: While the aforementioned studies have demonstrated the modulation of motor bias in response to sensing of ligand and change in motor speed with PMF or when exposed to starvation conditions, there is as yet no clear evidence of the chemosensory transduction system influencing the motor speed in E. coli.
evidence: This claim represents the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Glucose is the preferred carbon source for E. coli's growth.
source: For E. coli, glucose is the preferred carbon source for cell's growth and there exist detailed studies on the molecular mechanism of sensing and adaptation to the ligand (Hazelbauer and Engström, 1980; Lux et al., 1999; Feng et al., 1999; Li and Hazelbauer, 2004; Neumann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Glucose signaling is achieved through two independent pathways: through the phosphotransferase system (PTS) pathway and via the Trg-sensing pathway.
source: The signaling is achieved through two independent pathways: through the phosphotransferase system (PTS) pathway and via the Trg-sensing pathway.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The combined signals from the PTS and Trg pathways determines the phosphorylation state of CheA, which in turn determines the concentration of CheY-P, and therefore the motor bias.
source: The combined signals from the two pathways determines the phosphorylation state of CheA, which in turn determines the concentration of CheY-P, and therefore the motor bias.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: 2Dg is sensed by the Trg sensor but is not metabolized since cells do not grow in its presence.
source: Adler et al., 1973 have shown that 2Dg is sensed by the Trg sensor, but unlike glucose, are not metabolized since cells do not grow in its presence.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cells lacking Trg show chemotactic response to 2Dg only when grown in the presence of glycerol through the activation of mannose PTS pathway.
source: Further, cells lacking Trg show chemotactic response to 2Dg only when grown in the presence of glycerol through the activation of mannose PTS pathway (Adler and Epstein, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the presence of glucose, there is a sharp increase in rotation rate from an average speed of about 6 to 7.5 Hz at about 100 s and again a further increase to about 9 Hz at around 650 s.
source: Figure 2A and B presents the time evolution of the rotation speed of a single motor after the introduction of glucose and 2Dg, respectively. In case of glucose, there is a sharp increase in rotation rate from an average speed of about 6 to 7.5 Hz at about 100 s and again a further increase to about 9 Hz at around 650 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For 2Dg, the rotation speed remains unchanged for about 300 s after which there is a sudden increase in average speed from about 4 Hz to about 5.7 Hz.
source: In comparison, for 2Dg the rotation speed remains unchanged for about 300 s after which there is a sudden increase in average speed from about 4 Hz to about 5.7 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The increased speed in 2Dg is sustained for about 200 s after which it returns to the pre-stimulus levels.
source: The increased speed is sustained for about 200 s after which it returns to the pre-stimulus levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The step increases in motor speed range between 1.0 and 2.0 Hz, which are of magnitude similar to those observed in the resurrection experiments.
source: The step increases, which range between 1.0 and 2.0 Hz, are of magnitude similar to those observed in the resurrection experiments (Block and Berg, 1984; Blair and Berg, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the current study and comparison to cited prior research.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of stator units increases with time when glucose is introduced.
source: While there is no change in the intensity for a cell in MB, the intensity increases with time when glucose is introduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: On introduction of 2Dg, the intensity increases for a short duration (about 4–5 min) after which it falls to the pre-stimulus value.
source: Interestingly, on introduction of 2Dg, which is a non-metabolizable ligand, the intensity increases for a short duration (about 4–5 min) after which it falls to the pre-stimulus value.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The modulation in motor speed is caused by recruitment of stator units upon mere sensing of ligand.
source: This result matches with the change in motor speed (Figure 2D) confirming that the modulation in motor speed is indeed caused by recruitment of stator units upon mere sensing of ligand.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: An increase of 17% at 5 min and 20% increase at 10 min was observed in the fluorescence intensity for glucose relative to its pre-stimulus value.
source: An increase of 17% at 5 min and 20% increase at 10 min was observed in the fluorescence intensity for glucose relative to its pre-stimulus value.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A 14% increase was observed at 5 min for 2Dg after which the intensity decreased to its pre-stimulus value.
source: A slightly lower increase (14%) was observed at 5 min for 2Dg after which the intensity decreased to its pre-stimulus value.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was no discernible trend in the intensity value measured for cell exposed to MB.
source: As expected there was no discernible trend in the intensity value measured for cell exposed to MB.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The normalized fluorescent intensity values are proportional to motor speeds suggesting that stator elements are added following the introduction of the two ligands.
source: The normalized fluorescent intensity values in different motors for the three conditions and the corresponding normalized motor speeds are presented in Figure 3C. The intensity is proportional to motor speeds suggesting that stator elements are added following the introduction of the two ligands.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is no change in the membrane potential for NaMB and 2Dg and their values are very close.
source: While there is no change in the potential for NaMB and 2Dg and their values are very close, the intensity value in the presence of glucose is significantly higher.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The intensity value in the presence of glucose is significantly higher than NaMB and 2Dg.
source: While there is no change in the potential for NaMB and 2Dg and their values are very close, the intensity value in the presence of glucose is significantly higher.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The stator unit recruitment in the presence of 2Dg is independent of PMF and is caused solely by sensing of 2Dg.
source: This clearly demonstrates that the stator unit recruitment in the presence of 2Dg is independent of PMF and is caused solely by sensing of 2Dg.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the membrane potential measurements showing no change for 2Dg.

claim: For glucose, the increase in motor speed would be a combination of increased PMF and that due to sensing.
source: For glucose, the increase in motor speed would be a combination of increased PMF and that due to sensing.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the membrane potential measurements showing increased potential for glucose.

claim: In the presence of glucose, the run speed increased monotonically with almost a 50% increase (29.6±1.0µm/s) at 16.5 min compared to that measured at the start of the experiment (20.1±0.9µm/s).
source: In the presence of glucose, the run speed increased monotonically (Figure 3E) with almost a 50% increase (29.6±1.0µm/s, mean ± s.e.) at 16.5 min compared to that measured at the start of the experiment (20.1±0.9µ m/s).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In case of 2Dg, the run speed increased up to 6.5 min reaching a value identical to that observed for glucose at the same time, resulting in a 26% increase (25±1.4µm/s) compared to the speeds measured at the start of the experiment.
source: In case of 2Dg, the run speed increased upto 6.5 min reaching a value identical to that observed for glucose at the same time, resulting in a 26% increase (25±1.4µm/s) compared to the speeds measured at the start of the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At longer times, unlike in glucose, the run speed in 2Dg decreased and reached values observed at the start of the experiment.
source: However, at longer times, unlike in glucose, the run speed decreased and reached values observed at the start of the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the absence of ligands, the run speed showed negligible change with speed values ranging approximately between 18 and 21 μm/s for the entire duration of the experiment.
source: In the absence of ligands, the run speed showed negligible change with speed values ranging approximately between 18 and 21 μm/s for the entire duration of the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Sensing alone can enhance the run speed, albeit for a short duration, as observed in case of 2Dg.
source: These results indicate that sensing alone can enhance the run speed, albeit for a short duration, as observed in case of 2Dg.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the run speed data for 2Dg.

claim: Metabolism plays a role in sustaining a high run speed.
source: A further increase in run speed is observed in case of glucose suggesting that metabolism plays a role in sustaining a high run speed.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing glucose and 2Dg run speed data.

claim: Stator unit recruitment due to sensing alone can enhance the swimming speed of a population.
source: Clearly, the observations made on a single motor via tethered cell experiments indeed reflect in the population behavior wherein stator unit recruitment due to sensing alone can enhance the swimming speed of a population.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from both tethered cell and population-level experiments.

claim: In glucose, there was significant increase in the motor speed (about 30%) compared to the pre-stimulus value for the Δtrg mutant strain.
source: However, in glucose, there was significant increase in the motor speed (about 30%) compared to the pre-stimulus value.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F for the Δtrg strain.

claim: In the absence of the Trg sensor, the motor speed remains unaffected in the presence of 2Dg.
source: These results clearly show that in the absence of the Trg sensor, the motor speed remains unaffected in the presence of 2Dg thereby reconfirming the earlier observation that sensing alone can contribute to motor speed modulation.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the Δtrg mutant experiments.

claim: The Δtrg mutant strain exhibits increased PMF in glucose through metabolism although the ligand is not sensed.
source: The mutant strain exhibits increased PMF in glucose through metabolism although the ligand is not sensed.
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane potential data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For the Δtrg strain, there is no change in run speed in response to 2Dg, which is identical to that observed in MB, while there is a significant increase in the presence of glucose (about 50% increase).
source: This behavior is observed at the population level (Figure 4B), wherein there is no change in run speed in response to 2Dg, which is identical to that observed in MB, while there is a significant increase in the presence of glucose (about 50% increase).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For the ΔptsI mutant, there was a marginal increase in motor speed in the presence of glucose while no significant change was observed in the presence of 2Dg.
source: In order to estimate the role of metabolism in motor speed modulation, we performed the same set of experiments in mutants lacking the ptsI gene. There was a marginal increase in motor speed (Figure 3F) and run speed (Figure 4D) in the presence of glucose while no significant change was observed in the presence of 2Dg.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3F and 4D.

claim: The small increase in membrane potential measured for the ΔptsI mutant strain in the presence of glucose explains the marginal increase in the motor and run speed.
source: The small increase in membrane potential measured for the mutant strain in the presence of glucose explains the marginal increase in the motor and run speed.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the membrane potential and motor speed data for the ΔptsI strain.

claim: The trends in run speed for the ΔcheY mutant are very similar to those observed with WT in that the run speed increases monotonically with time in the presence of glucose while the speed first increases and then decreases in case of 2Dg.
source: The results of such experiments are shown in Figure 4F. The trends are very similar to those observed with WT (Figure 3E) in that the run speed increases monotonically with time in the presence of glucose while the speed first increases and then decreases in case of 2Dg.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CheY-P has no role in the observed modulation in motor speed and the observed speed increases are independent of switching events.
source: The similarity of the observed trend with WT indicates that CheY-P has no role in the observed modulation in motor speed and the observed speed increases are independent of switching events.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ΔcheY mutant experiments.

claim: E. coli modulates its motor bias in response to ligands.
source: It is well known that E. coli modulates its motor bias in response to ligands (Adler, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to foundational work.

claim: For glucose, sensing leads to the dephosphorylation of CheY-P which in turn reduces the motor reversals leading to smooth runs.
source: For example, in case of glucose, which is sensed via the Trg chemoreceptor, sensing leads to the dephosphorylation of CheY-P which in turn reduces the motor reversals leading to smooth runs.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Glucose is also sensed and consumed via the PTS pathway, which is known to regulate CheY-P, thereby altering the bias.
source: Glucose is also sensed and consumed via the PTS pathway, which is known to regulate CheY-P, thereby altering the bias.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The signals from the Trg receptor and the PTS pathway combine (additive) to determine the reversal frequency.
source: Neumann et al., 2012 have shown that the signals from the Trg receptor and the PTS pathway combine (additive) to determine the reversal frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In tethered cell experiments, where the torque is in the high load regime, the motor speed is proportional to the ion motive force in both proton and sodium-driven motors.
source: Previous studies have shown that in tethered cell experiments, where the torque is in the high load regime, the motor speed is proportional to the ion motive force in both proton and sodium-driven motors (Gabel and Berg, 2003; Sowa et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in motor output have been attributed to the change in the number of stator units, which are assembled from a mobile pool of MotB molecules over a timescale of minutes when the PMF is increased.
source: These changes in motor output have been attributed to the change in the number of stator units, which are assembled from a mobile pool of MotB molecules over a timescale of minutes when the PMF is increased (Reid et al., 2006; Leake et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For cases where the mechanical load is low, such as in bead assay with sub-micron sized beads, the motor output can also vary with the magnitude of the load due to load-dependent stator unit recruitment.
source: In contrast, for cases where the mechanical load is low, such as in bead assay with sub-micron sized beads, the motor output can also vary with the magnitude of the load due to load-dependent stator unit recruitment (Tipping et al., 2013a; Lele et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is no evidence hitherto that mere sensing of a ligand can directly influence the motor speed at a fixed mechanical load.
source: While these studies clearly indicate the role of metabolism and mechanical load in motor speed modulation via stator unit recruitment, there is no evidence hitherto that mere sensing of a ligand can directly influence the motor speed at a fixed mechanical load.
evidence: This claim represents the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The tethered cell experiments demonstrate the recruitment of stator units in response to sensing of a ligand and therefore suggest the existence of a pathway that links the sensor to the motor.
source: The tethered cell experiments reported here clearly demonstrate the recruitment of stator units in response to sensing of a ligand and therefore suggest the existence of a pathway that links the sensor to the motor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The increase in stator unit density at the motor in response to 2Dg led to a concomitant enhancement in motor speed and thereby the run speed in a population.
source: Our experiments show an increase in stator unit density at the motor in response to 2Dg, a non-metabolizable analog of glucose. This increase in stator unit density led to a concomitant enhancement in motor speed and thereby the run speed in a population.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the experiments with 2Dg.

claim: Since 2Dg is sensed by the Trg sensor, a signal for speed modulation is communicated to the motor from the sensor.
source: Since 2Dg is sensed by the Trg sensor, this indicates that a signal for speed modulation is communicated to the motor from the sensor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the 2Dg experiments.

claim: There was no change in membrane potential confirming the absence of role of metabolism in 2Dg response.
source: Further, there was no change in membrane potential confirming the absence of role of metabolism and thereby suggesting that any change in the motor speed is only due to the sensing mechanism.
evidence: This claim is based on membrane potential measurements for 2Dg.

claim: Deleting the trg gene eliminated changes in motor speed in the presence of 2Dg.
source: This was further confirmed by deleting the trg gene, which eliminated changes in motor speed in the presence of 2Dg.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the Δtrg mutant experiments.

claim: In case of glucose, the enhancement in motor speed is much greater compared to that in 2Dg due to the combined effect of sensing and metabolism, caused by an even greater recruitment of stator units.
source: In case of glucose, the enhancement in motor speed is much greater compared to that in 2Dg due to the combined effect of sensing and metabolism, caused by an even greater recruitment of stator units (as indicated by increased intensity of fluorescently tagged stator unit).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of glucose and 2Dg data.

claim: The increase in motor speed for glucose is due to glucose metabolism leading to increased PMF while that due to sensing is through the Trg receptor.
source: Here, the increase in motor speed is due to glucose metabolism leading to increased PMF (Schwarz-Linek et al., 2016) while that due to sensing is through the Trg receptor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the glucose experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: A small increase in motor speed was observed when the ΔptsI cell was exposed to glucose but changes were statistically insignificant in the presence of 2Dg.
source: A small increase in motor speed was observed when the cell was exposed to glucose but changes were statistically insignificant in the presence of 2Dg.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the ΔptsI mutant experiments.

claim: A smaller variance in rotation speed indicates an increased number of stator units, thereby making the motor rotation smoother.
source: An alternate method to characterize stator unit recruitment is to determine the variance in mean rotation rate of the motor as a function of the number of revolutions (Samuel and Berg, 1995; Samuel and Berg, 1996). Thus, a smaller variance would indicate an increased number of stator units, thereby making the motor rotation smoother.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The tethered cell experiment with the WT cells shows a decrease in variance when exposed to 2Dg compared to that in MB.
source: The tethered cell experiment with the WT cells shows clearly a decrease in variance when exposed to 2Dg (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and E) compared to that in MB.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The variance decreased even further when exposed to glucose indicating a higher recruitment of stator units due to the combined effect of metabolism and sensing.
source: The variance decreased even further when exposed to glucose indicating a higher recruitment of stator units due to the combined effect of metabolism and sensing (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Motor speed of a mutant lacking in cheY was measured in the presence of both 2Dg and glucose, and the observed motor speed modulation was identical to that for the WT indicating that CheY does not play role in stator unit recruitment.
source: To answer this question, motor speed of a mutant lacking in cheY was measured in the presence of both 2Dg and glucose. The observed motor speed modulation was identical to that for the WT indicating that CheY does not play role in stator unit recruitment.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the ΔcheY mutant experiments.

claim: There exists a signaling pathway, independent of the chemotaxis pathway, that links the sensor to the motor.
source: These observations clearly suggest that there exists a signaling pathway, independent of the chemotaxis pathway, that links the sensor to the motor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ΔcheY mutant experiments.

claim: In the cheY mutant, the bias is locked in the CCW direction and therefore is also always in the run mode.
source: Note that in the cheY mutant, the bias is locked in the CCW direction and therefore is also always in the run mode.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about cheY mutants.

claim: Experiments with WT cells show a momentary increase in CCW bias after which the bias recovers to the pre-stimulus value thereby demonstrating the well-known chemotactic response.
source: Experiments with WT cells on the other hand show a momentary increase in CCW bias after which the bias recovers to the pre-stimulus value thereby demonstrating the well-known chemotactic response.
evidence: This claim is based on data from WT experiments.

claim: When the cell is exposed to 2Dg, one or more stator units are recruited temporarily thereby increasing the rotation speed, and the stator units disengage within a short time (about 5–10 min) after which the rotation rate returns to the pre-stimulus values.
source: When the cell is exposed to 2Dg, one or more stator units are recruited temporarily (states 1–2 in Figure 5A, blue line) thereby increasing the rotation speed (see schematic in Figure 5B). The stator units disengage within a short time (about 5–10 min) after which the rotation rate returns to the pre-stimulus values (back to state 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: When the cell is exposed to glucose, the combined contribution from sensing and PMF leads to a much larger increase in the number of bound stator units and the speeds remain high for much longer time periods (over 15 min), due to the metabolism.
source: However, when the cell is exposed to glucose, a metabolite, the combined contribution from sensing and PMF leads to a much larger increase in the number of bound stator units (states 1–3, red line) and the speeds remain high for a much longer time periods (over 15 min), due to the metabolism.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The drift velocity of a population of cells in response to a ligand gradient is dependent on both the tumble frequency and the swimming speed.
source: At the population level, these results imply a more efficient chemotaxis response since the drift velocity of a population of cells in response to a ligand gradient is dependent on both the tumble frequency and the swimming speed.
evidence: This claim is based on established models of chemotaxis.

claim: The well-known RTBL model links the population-level chemotactic response to the individual microscopic variables of cell's swimming speed, persistence time, and temporal receptor occupation.
source: Specifically, the well-known RTBL model of Rivero et al., 1989, which is based on the Keller-Segel model, links the population-level chemotactic response to the individual microscopic variables of cell's swimming speed, persistence time, and temporal receptor occupation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The drift velocity is directly proportional to the product of the swimming speed and a function that depends on the tumbling frequency, spatial gradient of chemoattractant, and occupancy of chemoreceptor.
source: The drift velocity (also known as the chemotactic velocity) of the population is directly proportional to the product of the swimming speed and a function that depends on the tumbling frequency, spatial gradient of chemoattractant, and occupancy of chemoreceptor (Equation 22 of Rivero et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: For small gradients, the drift velocity varies as the square of the swimming speed.
source: For small gradients, the expression simplifies such that the drift velocity varies as the square of the swimming speed (Equation 25 of Rivero et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Even a 10% increase in the swimming speed could cause the drift velocity to increase anywhere between 10% and 20% leading to a significant improvement in the chemotactic efficiency.
source: These results imply that even a 10% increase in the swimming speed could cause the drift velocity to increase anywhere between 10% and 20% leading to a significant improvement in the chemotactic efficiency.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RTBL model.

claim: The pathway linking sensor to motor is independent of the known sensory transduction pathway since the observed speed modulation also occurs in the absence of CheY.
source: Finally, the pathway is independent of the known sensory transduction pathway since the observed speed modulation also occurs in the absence of CheY (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is based on data from the ΔcheY mutant experiments.

claim: c-di-GMP effector YcgR can inhibit flagellar motility by directly interacting with the motor to modulate both its bias and speed.
source: Recent studies have shown that c-di-GMP effector YcgR can inhibit flagellar motility by directly interacting with the motor to modulate both its bias and speed (Boehm et al., 2010; Paul et al., 2010; Nieto et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is no evidence that the YcgR mechanism can enhance motor speeds beyond pre-stimulus levels.
source: While the aforementioned mechanism has been shown to inhibit motor speeds, there is no evidence that the same can enhance motor speeds beyond pre-stimulus levels.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge regarding the YcgR mechanism.

claim: The results point to a sophisticated signaling network with multiple strategies to regulate motor behavior enabling an efficient response to changes in bacteria's environment.
source: Irrespective of the details of the mechanism, the results presented here point to a sophisticated signaling network with multiple strategies to regulate motor behavior enabling an efficient response to changes in bacteria's environment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overall findings of the study.

claim: E. coli RP437 and its four mutants were grown in tryptone media till mid-log phase at OD600 at 200 rpm, 30°C.
source: E. coli RP437 and its four mutants (see Table 1) were inoculated from glycerol stock into tryptone agar plates. A single colony isolate was grown overnight and then sub-cultured in 50 ml tryptone media (0.015 g/l; Sigma) till mid-log phase (OD600 at 200 rpm, 30°C).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Knockout mutant strains were developed by using standard site-specific recombination method for inactivation of genes.
source: Other knockout mutant strains were developed by using standard site-specific recombination method for inactivation of genes (Datsenko and Wanner, 2000; Baba et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods and is supported by citations.

claim: The desired gene was deleted by replacing it with kanamycin marker.
source: The desired gene was deleted by replacing it with kanamycin marker.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Use of silicone oil prior to antibody treatment resulted in a more stable interaction between anti-flagellin antibody and the glass slide.
source: Use of silicone oil prior to antibody treatment in our case resulted in a more stable interaction between anti-flagellin antibody and the glass slide.
evidence: This claim describes an observation from the experimental methods.

claim: Experiments with color dyes showed that a combination of convective flow induced by the incoming dye solution and accompanying diffusion led to the dye reaching the visualization region within 30–45 s of introducing the dye.
source: Experiments with color dyes showed that a combination of convective flow induced by the incoming dye solution and accompanying diffusion led to the dye reaching the visualization region within 30–45 s of introducing the dye.
evidence: This claim describes an observation from control experiments.

claim: The measured average swimming speed of 18.2 ± 7.9 μm/s and an average turn angle of 71° for RP437 cells dispersed uniformly in a microchannel containing plain MB are close to those observed for the same strain reported earlier, 18.8 ± 8.2 μm/s and 69°.
source: The measured average swimming speed of 18.2 ± 7.9 μm/s (average ± standard deviation) and an average turn angle of 71° for RP437 cells dispersed uniformly in a microchannel containing plain MB are close to those observed for the same strain reported earlier, 18.8 ± 8.2 μm/s and 69°, by Saragosti et al., 2011.
evidence: This claim validates the experimental methods by comparison to prior research.

claim: DiOC2(3) is a lipophilic cationic dye and was used as a membrane potential probe.
source: 3,3-Diethyloxacarbocyanine iodide ((DiOC2(3)) from ThermoFisher Scientific) is a lipophilic cationic dye and was used as a membrane potential probe.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The ratio of red and green fluorescence (R/G) eliminates the dependence on cell size and directly correlates with the membrane potential of the cells.
source: The ratio of red and green fluorescence (R/G) eliminates the dependence on cell size and directly correlates with the membrane potential of the cells.
evidence: This claim describes the rationale for the measurement method.

claim: CCCP is an ionophore which increases membrane permeability to protons and thereby eliminates membrane potential.
source: CCCP is an ionophore which increases membrane permeability to protons and thereby eliminates membrane potential.
evidence: This claim describes the function of a control reagent used in the study.
